question: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and what problem does it solve?
directAnswer: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a pattern where, instead of relying only on what a language model learned during training, you first retrieve relevant documents from an external knowledge source and then insert them into the model's prompt so it can answer using that fresh, specific context. It solves the core limitations of a bare LLM: its knowledge is frozen at training time, it cannot see your private or proprietary data, and it tends to hallucinate when asked about things it does not know. By grounding answers in retrieved text, RAG makes responses more accurate, up to date, and traceable to sources.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
RAG is a two-stage pipeline. First a retriever finds passages relevant to the user's question, typically by embedding the query and searching a vector store for the nearest chunks. Second a generator (the LLM) receives a prompt that contains both the question and those retrieved passages, and writes an answer grounded in them. A minimal flow looks like:
query -> embed -> vector search -> top-k chunks -> build prompt(question + chunks) -> LLM -> answer
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A pretrained model bakes knowledge into its weights, which means it cannot learn new facts without retraining, cannot access data it never saw such as your internal wiki, and has no reliable way to cite where an answer came from. RAG exists to decouple knowledge from the model: you keep the reasoning ability of the LLM but supply the facts at inference time from a source you control and can update instantly.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Offline, you ingest documents, split them into chunks, embed each chunk into a vector, and store those vectors in an index. Online, you embed the incoming query, retrieve the most similar chunks by vector similarity (often combined with keyword search), optionally rerank them, and assemble a prompt that instructs the model to answer using only the provided context. The model then generates an answer, ideally with citations pointing back to the retrieved chunks.

whyImportant: RAG is the default architecture for building LLM applications over private or fast-changing data, so it is almost always the opening question in an AI-engineering interview. Being able to explain the retrieve-then-generate split, and why it beats a bare model for factual and proprietary questions, shows you understand where LLMs get their knowledge and how to make them reliable in production.
realWorldExample: A customer-support assistant needs to answer questions about a product whose documentation changes weekly. Instead of fine-tuning a model every week, the team indexes the current docs in a vector store. When a user asks 'How do I rotate my API key?', the system retrieves the relevant help articles and passes them to the model, which produces an accurate answer citing the exact article, even though that article did not exist when the model was trained.

nestedTopics.title: Retrieval versus generation
nestedTopics.explanation: RAG cleanly separates finding information from expressing it. The retriever is responsible for surfacing the right facts, and the generator is responsible for composing a fluent, correct answer from those facts. Weakness in either stage hurts the final result, which is why RAG evaluation looks at retrieval quality and generation quality separately.

nestedTopics.title: Grounding and reduced hallucination
nestedTopics.explanation: Because the model is told to answer from supplied context, it is far less likely to invent facts than when answering from memory alone. Grounding also enables citations, since each claim can be tied to a specific retrieved chunk, which builds user trust and makes answers auditable.

nestedTopics.title: The indexing pipeline
nestedTopics.explanation: Before any query can be served, documents must be ingested, chunked, embedded, and stored. This offline pipeline determines what the system can ever retrieve, so choices about chunking and embeddings made here shape the quality of every future answer.

followUps.question: Does RAG change the model's weights?
followUps.answer: No. RAG leaves the model's weights completely untouched; it only changes what goes into the prompt at inference time. The model's parameters, and therefore its reasoning and language abilities, stay exactly as they were after training. What changes is the context window, which now carries retrieved facts the model can read and use. This is a key advantage: you can update the knowledge base instantly by re-indexing documents, with no retraining, no GPU cost, and no risk of degrading the model's general capabilities.

followUps.question: What are the main failure points of a RAG system?
followUps.answer: The two big ones map to the two stages. Retrieval can fail by returning irrelevant chunks, missing the chunk that actually contains the answer, or returning a chunk that was split in a way that cut off the needed information. Generation can fail by ignoring the provided context, blending in memorized but wrong facts, or misreading the retrieved passages. There are also upstream failures in the indexing pipeline, such as poor chunking or stale embeddings, which silently degrade everything downstream. Good RAG systems measure retrieval and generation quality separately so you can tell which stage is at fault.

question: What are embeddings and how does cosine similarity measure semantic closeness?
directAnswer: An embedding is a fixed-length vector of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, produced by an embedding model. Texts with similar meanings map to vectors that point in similar directions in this high-dimensional space, even if they share no words. Cosine similarity measures how aligned two vectors are by computing the cosine of the angle between them: it equals the dot product divided by the product of the vectors' magnitudes, giving a score from -1 to 1 where 1 means identical direction. RAG uses embeddings plus cosine similarity to find chunks whose meaning is close to the query's meaning rather than relying on exact keyword matches.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
An embedding model turns text into a vector, for example a 1536-dimensional array of floats. Cosine similarity between two vectors a and b is:
cos_sim(a, b) = dot(a, b) / (norm(a) * norm(b))
A score near 1 means the texts are semantically close; near 0 means unrelated; negative means opposed in direction.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Keyword search misses meaning: 'car' and 'automobile' never match despite being synonyms, and 'How do I reset my password?' will not match a doc titled 'Recovering account access' by words alone. Embeddings capture semantics so related ideas land near each other, and cosine similarity gives a cheap, scale-invariant way to rank how close two meanings are.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The embedding model is trained so that semantically similar inputs produce nearby vectors. To compare two texts you embed both and compute cosine similarity. Cosine is preferred over raw dot product when you care about direction rather than magnitude, since it normalizes out vector length; in fact if vectors are unit-normalized, cosine similarity and dot product are identical, which is why many vector stores normalize embeddings and then use dot product for speed.

whyImportant: Embeddings are the foundation of the retrieval half of RAG, so interviewers check that you understand what they represent and how similarity is scored. Knowing that cosine measures angle, not distance, and understanding the normalization relationship to dot product, signals you can reason about retrieval quality and vector-store configuration rather than treating embeddings as a black box.
realWorldExample: In a documentation search, a user types 'app keeps crashing on startup'. The query embedding lands near the embedding of a support article titled 'Troubleshooting application launch failures' even though they share almost no words. Cosine similarity ranks that article above a keyword-only match like an unrelated page that happens to contain the word 'app', because the article's meaning is closer to the query's meaning.

nestedTopics.title: Semantic versus lexical matching
nestedTopics.explanation: Lexical matching compares surface words; semantic matching via embeddings compares meaning. Embeddings let synonyms, paraphrases, and related concepts match, which is why dense retrieval can find relevant passages that a keyword search would miss entirely.

nestedTopics.title: Cosine versus Euclidean versus dot product
nestedTopics.explanation: Cosine measures the angle between vectors and ignores their length, Euclidean measures straight-line distance, and dot product combines both angle and magnitude. For text embeddings, cosine is the common default because it is length-invariant; when embeddings are normalized to unit length, dot product gives the same ranking as cosine but is faster to compute.

nestedTopics.title: Dimensionality and model choice
nestedTopics.explanation: Embedding models output vectors of a fixed dimension, and different models trade off quality, cost, and speed. Higher dimensions can capture more nuance but cost more to store and search, and you must use the same model to embed both documents and queries so their vectors live in the same space.

followUps.question: Why must you use the same embedding model for documents and queries?
followUps.answer: Because embeddings from different models live in different, incomparable vector spaces. Each model learns its own geometry, so the vector one model produces for a query has no meaningful relationship to the vector a different model produced for your documents; cosine similarity between them would be noise. To retrieve correctly, the query and the stored chunks must be embedded by the same model (and the same version), so they occupy the same space and similarity actually reflects semantic closeness. If you ever switch embedding models, you have to re-embed your entire corpus, not just new queries.

followUps.question: If vectors are normalized, why do many systems use dot product instead of cosine?
followUps.answer: When every vector is normalized to unit length, the denominator in the cosine formula becomes 1, so cosine similarity reduces exactly to the dot product. That means you get identical rankings but skip the per-comparison division and magnitude computation, which is meaningfully faster at scale when you are scoring millions of vectors. So vector stores often normalize embeddings once at insert time and then use plain dot product for search. The result is mathematically equivalent to cosine while being cheaper, which is why 'cosine' and 'normalized dot product' are effectively interchangeable in practice.

question: Why split documents into chunks, and what makes a good chunk?
directAnswer: You split documents into chunks because embedding models and LLM context windows both work better on focused, bounded pieces of text than on whole documents. A single long document contains many topics, so embedding it as one vector blurs its meaning and makes precise retrieval impossible; chunking lets each vector represent one coherent idea. A good chunk is large enough to be self-contained and understandable on its own, small enough to embed cleanly and fit several into the prompt, and ideally aligned to natural boundaries like paragraphs or sections rather than cut arbitrarily mid-sentence. Overlap between adjacent chunks helps preserve context that would otherwise be lost at the split point.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Chunking is the step that turns raw documents into the retrievable units of a RAG index. For example, a 40-page manual might become a few hundred chunks of roughly 500 tokens each, with a small overlap so a fact spanning a boundary appears in both neighbors. Each chunk is embedded and stored separately.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Embedding an entire document into one vector averages away specifics, so a query about one detail cannot find it. And even if you could retrieve a whole document, stuffing it into the prompt wastes the context window and dilutes the model's attention with irrelevant text. Chunking exists to make retrieval precise (find exactly the passage that answers the question) and generation efficient (feed only relevant, compact context).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A chunker walks through the text and emits pieces bounded by a size limit, ideally breaking at semantic boundaries such as headings, paragraphs, or sentences. Overlap is added by starting each new chunk a bit before the previous one ended, so context near boundaries is not orphaned. The right size and overlap depend on the content and the embedding model, and are tuned by evaluating retrieval quality.

whyImportant: Chunking quietly determines the ceiling on retrieval quality: if the answer never sits cleanly in a retrievable chunk, no amount of clever search or reranking can recover it. Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand that RAG quality is decided largely in the indexing pipeline, not just at query time, and whether you can reason about the size-versus-context tradeoff.
realWorldExample: A legal-document assistant indexes contracts. If chunks are too large, a query about an indemnification clause retrieves a chunk mixing indemnification with five unrelated clauses, diluting relevance and wasting prompt space. If chunks are too small, a single clause gets split so the retrieved piece lacks the definitions it references. Chunking at clause boundaries with modest overlap keeps each clause self-contained and its context intact, so retrieval returns exactly the relevant, complete provision.

nestedTopics.title: Self-containment
nestedTopics.explanation: A good chunk should make sense read on its own, because at retrieval time the model sees the chunk without the surrounding document. Chunks that depend on earlier context, like a pronoun whose antecedent was split off, retrieve poorly and confuse the model.

nestedTopics.title: Overlap between chunks
nestedTopics.explanation: Overlap repeats a small tail of one chunk at the start of the next so that a fact or sentence straddling a boundary is fully present in at least one chunk. It costs some storage and redundancy but reduces the chance of splitting an answer across two pieces where neither is retrievable alone.

nestedTopics.title: Boundary-aware splitting
nestedTopics.explanation: Splitting on natural structure such as paragraphs, headings, or sentences produces more coherent chunks than a fixed character count that cuts mid-word or mid-sentence. Structure-aware chunkers preserve meaning and improve both embedding quality and readability of the retrieved context.

followUps.question: What goes wrong if chunks are too large?
followUps.answer: Overly large chunks mix multiple topics into one vector, so the embedding becomes an average that represents none of them precisely. A query about a specific detail then matches the chunk only weakly, and other, more focused chunks may outrank it, hurting recall. Even when a big chunk is retrieved, it fills the prompt with mostly irrelevant text, wasting context-window budget and diluting the model's attention, which can lower answer quality. You also fit fewer distinct chunks into the prompt, reducing the diversity of evidence the model sees.

followUps.question: What goes wrong if chunks are too small?
followUps.answer: Tiny chunks often lack the surrounding context needed to be understood, so a retrieved fragment might reference a term defined a sentence earlier that got split away, leaving the model unable to interpret it. Small chunks also fragment a single answer across several pieces, so you must retrieve and correctly assemble multiple chunks to reconstruct one fact, which raises the chance of missing part of it. And they inflate the index size and the number of near-duplicate matches. The fix is usually a moderate size with overlap, tuned by measuring retrieval quality on real queries.

question: What is a vector store and how does it retrieve the top-k most similar chunks?
directAnswer: A vector store is a database specialized for storing embedding vectors and answering nearest-neighbor queries: given a query vector, it returns the k stored vectors most similar to it under a chosen metric like cosine or dot product. In RAG it holds the embedding of every chunk along with the chunk's text and metadata, so at query time you embed the question, ask the store for the top-k nearest chunks, and feed those to the model. The store's job is to make this similarity search fast even over millions of vectors, which it does using approximate nearest-neighbor indexes rather than comparing against every vector.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
A vector store maps each chunk to (vector, text, metadata) and supports a query like 'give me the 5 chunks whose vectors are closest to this query vector'. Popular examples include FAISS, pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate, and Qdrant. Conceptually:
store.add(id, vector, text, metadata)
results = store.search(query_vector, k=5)
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A brute-force top-k over every vector is exact but O(n) per query, which becomes too slow for large corpora and high query rates. Vector stores exist to provide sub-linear approximate search, plus the operational features a real system needs: persistence, updates, metadata filtering, and scaling. They make semantic retrieval practical at production scale.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: At insert time the store places each vector into an index structure such as HNSW (a navigable small-world graph) or an IVF scheme (clustering vectors into lists). At query time it navigates that structure to find likely-nearest candidates without scanning everything, then returns the top-k by the configured similarity metric. Because the index is approximate, it trades a small amount of recall for a large speedup, and parameters let you tune that tradeoff.

whyImportant: The vector store is the engine of retrieval, so interviewers want to know you understand what it does, why exact search does not scale, and that approximate indexes trade recall for speed. This knowledge underlies decisions about which store to use, how to configure the index, and how to combine vector search with metadata filters, all of which affect real system performance.
realWorldExample: A knowledge base with two million documentation chunks serves thousands of queries per minute. A brute-force scan of two million vectors per query would be far too slow, so the team uses an HNSW index in the vector store, which returns the top-8 chunks in a few milliseconds with over 95 percent recall. They also attach metadata like product and version to each chunk so a query can be filtered to only the relevant product before similarity ranking.

nestedTopics.title: Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN)
nestedTopics.explanation: ANN indexes like HNSW and IVF find vectors that are very likely among the true nearest neighbors without comparing against every stored vector. They accept a small drop in recall in exchange for a large speedup, and tuning parameters lets you move along that speed-versus-recall curve.

nestedTopics.title: Metadata filtering
nestedTopics.explanation: Beyond pure similarity, vector stores let you attach metadata to each chunk and filter on it, for example restricting search to a specific tenant, document type, or date range. Combining a filter with vector search narrows results to those that are both relevant and permitted.

nestedTopics.title: Storing text and metadata alongside vectors
nestedTopics.explanation: The store keeps not just the vector but the original chunk text and identifiers, so a search returns everything needed to build the prompt and to cite the source. This colocation is what lets a single query go from question to grounded, attributable context.

followUps.question: What is the difference between exact and approximate nearest-neighbor search?
followUps.answer: Exact search compares the query against every stored vector and is guaranteed to return the true top-k, but its cost grows linearly with the number of vectors, so it becomes too slow for large corpora or high query volumes. Approximate nearest-neighbor search uses an index such as HNSW or IVF to examine only a promising subset of vectors, returning results that are almost always the true nearest neighbors in a fraction of the time. The tradeoff is a small, tunable loss of recall for a large gain in speed. For most production RAG systems the recall loss is negligible and the speedup is essential, so ANN is the default; exact search is reserved for small collections or when perfect recall is required.

followUps.question: Why attach metadata to vectors instead of only storing the embedding?
followUps.answer: Metadata lets you constrain and contextualize retrieval in ways pure similarity cannot. Filtering by fields like tenant, product, language, or timestamp ensures you only retrieve chunks the user is allowed to see or that are relevant to their context, which is essential for multi-tenant security and for scoping answers to the right document set. Metadata also carries the source identifiers needed to build citations, so the answer can point back to the exact document and location. Without metadata you would retrieve semantically similar but possibly forbidden, outdated, or unattributable chunks, so it is central to correctness, access control, and trust.

question: What does it mean to ground an answer in retrieved context and provide citations?
directAnswer: Grounding means the model composes its answer strictly from the retrieved passages you supplied, rather than from its own memorized knowledge, so every claim is backed by evidence that is actually in the prompt. Citations make that grounding visible by tagging each part of the answer with a reference to the specific retrieved chunk or source it came from. Together they turn an opaque generated answer into a verifiable one: users can check the cited source, and the system is far less likely to hallucinate because it is instructed to stay within the provided context and to say when the context does not contain the answer.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Grounding is enforced through the prompt: you give the model the retrieved chunks, label them with identifiers, and instruct it to answer only from those chunks and to cite the identifiers it used. For example the prompt says 'Using only the sources below, answer the question and cite sources like [1], [2]. If the answer is not in the sources, say you do not know.' The output then reads like 'Rotate the key from Settings > API [2].'
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A model answering from memory can be confidently wrong and gives users no way to verify it. Grounding exists to tie answers to a controllable, current knowledge base, and citations exist to make answers auditable and to build trust. In regulated or high-stakes domains, an unverifiable answer is often unusable, so grounding and citation are requirements, not niceties.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each retrieved chunk is included in the prompt with a stable label (a number or source id). The instruction constrains the model to use only that context and to attach labels to its claims. At the end you can validate the output: check that cited labels correspond to real retrieved chunks, and optionally that the cited chunk actually supports the sentence. Answers that the context cannot support should trigger an 'I don't know' rather than a fabricated response.

whyImportant: Grounding and citation are what make RAG trustworthy enough to deploy, so interviewers probe whether you understand that a fluent answer is not the same as a correct one. Demonstrating that you constrain the model to the context, handle the 'not in the sources' case, and validate citations shows you can build systems that are accountable rather than just plausible-sounding.
realWorldExample: A medical-information assistant answers a clinician's question and appends citations to the exact guideline paragraphs it used, so the clinician can click through and confirm the recommendation before acting. When a question falls outside the indexed guidelines, the assistant is instructed to respond that it lacks a grounded source rather than guess, which prevents a dangerous hallucinated recommendation and keeps the human in control.

nestedTopics.title: Answer only from context
nestedTopics.explanation: The prompt explicitly restricts the model to the supplied passages, discouraging it from filling gaps with memorized or invented facts. This is the primary lever for reducing hallucination and is what makes citations meaningful, since a cited claim should be traceable to the referenced chunk.

nestedTopics.title: Handling the unknown case
nestedTopics.explanation: A grounded system must gracefully say it cannot answer when the retrieved context does not contain the information, instead of guessing. Explicit 'if not in the sources, say you do not know' instructions convert silent hallucinations into honest abstentions, which is safer and more trustworthy.

nestedTopics.title: Citation validation
nestedTopics.explanation: Beyond asking for citations, robust systems verify them: they confirm the cited ids exist among the retrieved chunks and can even re-check that the cited text supports the claim. This guards against the model citing a source that does not actually back what it said.

followUps.question: How do citations reduce hallucination in practice?
followUps.answer: Requiring citations forces the model to point at a specific supplied passage for each claim, which nudges it to make claims only when supporting text is present and gives you a way to catch it when it does not. If a sentence cites a chunk, you can verify the chunk actually supports it; if a sentence makes a claim with no citation, that is a signal it may be ungrounded. This visibility does not make the model perfect, but it converts silent fabrication into something detectable and lets you enforce 'no citation, no claim' policies. Combined with an instruction to abstain when the context lacks the answer, citations meaningfully cut down confident wrong answers and make the remaining ones auditable.

followUps.question: What should a grounded system do when retrieval returns nothing relevant?
followUps.answer: It should abstain rather than answer from the model's parametric memory. The correct behavior is to detect that the retrieved context does not support an answer, either because retrieval returned nothing or returned low-relevance chunks, and respond that the information is not available in the knowledge base, optionally suggesting how the user might rephrase or where else to look. This is far safer than letting the model improvise, which reintroduces exactly the hallucination risk RAG is meant to prevent. Well-designed systems set a relevance threshold on retrieval scores and treat below-threshold results as 'no answer found', keeping the assistant honest about the limits of its grounded knowledge.

question: When should you use RAG versus fine-tuning versus a long-context prompt?
directAnswer: Use RAG when the model needs access to a large, changing, or private body of factual knowledge, because you can update the knowledge base instantly and keep answers grounded and citable without retraining. Use fine-tuning when you need to change the model's behavior, style, format, or specialized skill rather than its facts, since fine-tuning teaches patterns but is a poor way to inject frequently changing facts. Use a long-context prompt when the relevant material is small enough to fit in the context window and is specific to this one request, since stuffing everything in is simplest when it fits. In many real systems these combine: fine-tune for behavior, use RAG for knowledge, and rely on the context window to carry the retrieved material.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: These are three ways to give a model information or capability. RAG retrieves relevant facts at inference and puts them in the prompt. Fine-tuning adjusts the model's weights on example data. A long-context prompt simply places all needed material directly into the request. Each targets a different problem: knowledge, behavior, and one-shot bulk context respectively.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: No single mechanism covers every need. Facts change too often and are too voluminous to bake into weights, so RAG exists for knowledge. Some needs are about how the model responds, not what it knows, so fine-tuning exists for behavior and style. And sometimes you just have a document you want the model to consider right now, so long-context exists for direct, transient input.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: RAG keeps knowledge external and current, retrieving only what each query needs, which keeps prompts small and answers grounded. Fine-tuning shifts the model's default outputs toward your examples but does not give reliable factual recall and requires retraining to update. Long-context loads everything into the window, which is simple but costs tokens on every call, can exceed limits, and can suffer from the model attending poorly to information buried in the middle of a very long input.

whyImportant: This tradeoff is one of the most common AI-engineering interview questions because choosing the wrong tool wastes money and produces unreliable systems. Demonstrating that facts belong in RAG, behavior belongs in fine-tuning, and only small transient material belongs in a long-context prompt shows mature judgment about system design rather than reaching for whichever technique is trendy.
realWorldExample: A company wants an assistant that answers questions about its constantly updated internal policies in a specific formal tone. The right design fine-tunes a small model to adopt the tone and format, uses RAG to pull the current policy passages so answers stay accurate as policies change, and lets the retrieved passages ride in the context window. Trying to fine-tune the policies themselves would mean retraining on every policy edit and would still risk the model misremembering details.

nestedTopics.title: Knowledge versus behavior
nestedTopics.explanation: The cleanest way to choose is to ask whether the gap is about what the model knows or how it behaves. Missing or changing facts call for RAG; wrong style, format, or task-specific skill calls for fine-tuning. Conflating the two, such as fine-tuning to teach facts, leads to brittle, hard-to-update systems.

nestedTopics.title: Freshness and update cost
nestedTopics.explanation: RAG updates by re-indexing documents, which is cheap and immediate, so it suits fast-changing knowledge. Fine-tuning updates by retraining, which is slow and expensive, so it suits stable behaviors. Long-context updates trivially per request but pays token cost every single call and cannot exceed the window.

nestedTopics.title: Combining approaches
nestedTopics.explanation: These are not mutually exclusive. Production systems often fine-tune for consistent behavior, use RAG to supply current facts, and use the context window to carry the retrieved chunks. Thinking of them as complementary layers rather than competitors usually yields the best design.

followUps.question: Why is fine-tuning a poor choice for frequently changing facts?
followUps.answer: Fine-tuning bakes information into the model's weights, so updating a fact means gathering new training data and retraining, which is slow, expensive, and cannot be done on every document edit. Worse, fine-tuning teaches patterns and tendencies rather than a reliable lookup table, so the model may still misremember or blend facts, and it gives no citation or way to verify where an answer came from. For knowledge that changes often, RAG is strictly better: you re-index the changed documents in seconds, answers stay grounded and current, and you can cite the exact source. Fine-tuning shines for durable behaviors like tone and output format, not for volatile facts.

followUps.question: If context windows keep getting larger, does that make RAG unnecessary?
followUps.answer: Not really. Even with very large windows, putting an entire corpus into every prompt is costly because you pay for those tokens on every call, and it can hurt quality since models often attend less reliably to information buried in the middle of a very long input. RAG keeps prompts small and focused by retrieving only the relevant passages, which is cheaper, faster, and often more accurate than dumping everything in. Large context does make RAG easier by letting you include more retrieved chunks and bigger ones, and it helps when the relevant material is modest and fits comfortably, but for large, changing, or access-controlled knowledge bases, targeted retrieval remains the practical and economical choice.
